items.snippet_en: The CDC states that COVID-19 vaccines do not contain microchips and are designed to stimulate an immune response, not to track individuals.
The Mayo Clinic explicitly states that COVID-19 vaccines do not contain microchips.
The Wellness Coalition states that COVID-19 vaccines do not contain microchips and are designed to stimulate an immune response, not to track individuals.
MyMLC.com states that COVID-19 vaccines do not contain microchips.
The microchip conspiracy theory gained traction from misinterpretations of comments made by Bill Gates about digital vaccine records and misrepresentations of RFID chips used on vaccine vials.

Experts explain that it would be impossible to fit a microchip, power source, and transmission capabilities into the small gauge needle used for vaccinations. The microchip conspiracy theory gained traction from misrepresentations of RFID chips used on vaccine vials.
FactCheck.org states that COVID-19 vaccines do not have patient tracking devices. The microchip conspiracy theory gained traction from misinterpretations of comments made by Bill Gates.
KSAT.com discusses the claim that the COVID-19 vaccine contains a tracking device, noting the microchip conspiracy theory gained traction from misinterpretations of comments made by Bill Gates.

Experts explain that it would be impossible to fit a microchip into the small gauge needle used for vaccinations. This claim has been widely circulated on social media, with some videos falsely purporting to show microchips in vaccines.
FactCheck.org clarifies that the Pfizer CEO was not referencing COVID-19 vaccines in posts about microchips. The ingredients of COVID-19 vaccines are publicly available and do not include microchips.

Halodoc.com discusses misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines. The ingredients of COVID-19 vaccines are publicly available and do not include microchips. This claim has been widely circulated on social media, with some videos falsely demonstrating magnetic effects on vaccinated arms.

The Indonesian Ministry of Health (Kemkes.go.id) addresses the hoax that COVID-19 vaccines contain magnetic microchips. This claim has been widely circulated on social media, with some videos falsely demonstrating magnetic effects on vaccinated arms.

AFP Fact Check debunks the claim that COVID-19 vaccines contain microchips. This claim has been widely circulated on social media, with some videos falsely demonstrating magnetic effects on vaccinated arms.
